etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English coward, from Old French coart, cuard ( > French couard), from coue (“tail”), coe + -ard (pejorative agent noun suffix); coue, coe is in turn from Latin cauda. The reference seems to be to an animal "turning tail", or having its tail between its legs, especially a dog. Compare the expression tail between one's legs. Unrelated to English cower. Displaced native Old English earg (surviving in northern dialect English argh).

quote.citation: c. 1599, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Ivlivs Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies, London: Printed by Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, act II, scene ii, page 117, column 1:
quote.text: Cowards dye many times before their deaths, / The valiant neuer taſte of death but once:  […]

quote.citation: 1856: Gustave Flaubert, Madame Bovary, Part II Chapter IV, translated by Eleanor Marx-Aveling
quote.text: He tortured himself to find out how he could make his declaration to her, and always halting between the fear of displeasing her and the shame of being such a coward, he wept with discouragement and desire. Then he took energetic resolutions, wrote letters that he tore up, put it off to times that he again deferred.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 17, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: It is a coward and servile humour, for a man to disguise and hide himselfe under a maske, and not dare to shew himselfe as he is.

quote.citation: c. 1605, William Shakespeare, King Lear, Act II, Scene 4,[1]
quote.text: He rais’d the house with loud and coward cries.

quote.citation: 1709, Matthew Prior, “Celia to Damon”, in Poems on Several Occasions‎[2], 2nd edition, London: Jacob Tonson, page 89:
quote.text: Invading Fears repel my Coward Joy;And Ills foreseen the pleasant Bliss destroy.

definitions.definition: (heraldry, of a lion) Borne in the escutcheon with his tail doubled between his legs.

quote.text: The first he coped with was their captain, whom / His sword sent headless to seek out a tomb. / This cowarded the valour of the rest,  […]
